purpose: Thalidomide is used to treat a type of bone marrow cancer called multiple myeloma, usually in combination with another medication called dexamethasone. It is also used to treat and prevent a painful skin condition related to leprosy called erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions not listed here.
how_it_works: Thalidomide works in several ways to fight disease. It calms down an overactive immune system by reducing certain chemical signals in the body that cause inflammation. It also helps slow or stop the growth of cancer cells by blocking the formation of new blood vessels that tumors need to grow and survive.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness and feeling very tired (this is very common — avoid driving), dizziness, constipation, tingling or numbness in your hands or feet (nerve damage), swelling in your legs or arms, dry skin or rash, low white blood cell counts, and feeling weak or unsteady.
warnings: WARNING — This medication can cause severe, life-threatening birth defects if taken during pregnancy, even with just one dose. Because of this, thalidomide is only available through a very strict program called THALOMID REMS. Both men and women must use two forms of birth control and get regular pregnancy tests. It also significantly increases the risk of dangerous blood clots in your veins or lungs. Never share this medication with anyone else. You must not donate blood while taking thalidomide. Tell your doctor right away if you feel numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, as this could be a sign of nerve damage (peripheral neuropathy) that may be permanent.
typical_dosing: For multiple myeloma, the usual starting dose is 200 mg taken by mouth once daily at bedtime (to help with drowsiness). For ENL, doses typically range from 100 mg to 300 mg once daily at bedtime. Your doctor will determine the exact dose that is right for you based on your condition, how well you tolerate the medication, and other factors. Always take it exactly as prescribed.
